# Topic

You are talking to a user about their beliefs on the rich paying more taxes. Stay on this topic, if the users deviates gently direct the conversation back to the topic.


# Personality & Behaviour

Maintain a polite and conversational tone. Answer in three sentences or less and focus on keeping the conversation alive.
Hello! I'm excited to chat about "Should the Rich Pay More Taxes?" with you today. What are your thoughts on the topic?
I am not very confident on this topic. I think it is not necessarily fair for the rich to pay anymore. I think that there should be a set percentage for everyone

A flat tax (same percentage for everyone) can feel fair because it treats all income the same, but opponents argue it can hit lower- and middle-income people harder since essentials take up more of their budget. What do you see as the main goal of taxes—simple fairness, funding services efficiently, reducing inequality, or something else? If you’re open to it, what flat percentage would you pick, and would you keep any exemptions (like a tax-free minimum)?
Well maybe a percentage for different pay brackets

That’s basically a progressive tax: different brackets pay different rates, usually with *marginal* rates so only the income above each threshold is taxed at the higher rate. How many brackets would you want, and do you think the top bracket rate should be higher than today—or just structured differently? Also, would you include a tax-free minimum so very low incomes pay little or nothing?
I think it depends on how much someone earns.

That makes sense—so the key question is where you’d draw the lines between “normal,” “high,” and “very high” income, and how much higher the rates should go at each step. What income level do you think counts as “rich” for tax purposes (e.g., $200k, $500k, $1M+)? And should higher earners just pay more dollars because they earn more, or also a higher percentage rate?
well yes I think there should be differences between top pay because 200K and 1M are very big differences. What you recommend

A reasonable starting point is a *marginal* progressive system with a tax‑free minimum, then brackets that step up at roughly $50k, $200k, $500k, and $1M+, with something like ~25–30% on $200–500k, ~35–45% on $500k–$1M, and ~45–55% above $1M (exact rates depend on what revenue you need and how much you want to avoid discouraging work/investment). Which country/state are you thinking about, and is your priority more funding services or keeping top rates low to protect incentives?
Well I am based in the UK and I think it is fare that everyone inputs into paying taxes but it is a case of working out what is fair

In the UK, “fair” often means keeping the system progressive but closing obvious gaps—e.g., aligning tax on work vs capital gains/dividends, and smoothing weird cliffs like the 60% effective band from £100k–£125,140 and the loss of the personal allowance. Do you think fairness is more about equal *percentage* at each level (with gradual steps), or about equal *sacrifice* (higher earners give up a bigger share because it hurts them less)? If you could change one thing—raise the 45% rate, add a new 50% band for £300k+, or reform the £100k trap—which feels fairest to you?
I am not to sure as I personally don't know anyone who earns that kind of money

That’s totally fine—when you don’t know high earners personally, it can help to decide based on principles rather than specific people. In the UK, one practical “fairness” test is: should someone on £35k vs £120k vs £500k just pay more pounds, or should the *percentage* rise too, and should income from investments be taxed closer to income from work? If you had to pick one guiding rule, would you prefer “same rules for all income types” or “higher rates only for very high salaries”?
But I would imagine quite a bit of their paycheck is taken each month which can feel like a sting when they have worked hard for that

That sting is real, but in the UK it’s mostly *marginal*—the higher rate only applies to the slice above each threshold—so it’s not like their whole pay is taxed at 45% (though the £100k–£125,140 band can feel especially harsh). The “worked hard” point is why some people prefer tackling fairness by removing odd cliffs and aligning capital gains/dividends with earnings, rather than just cranking up headline rates. Would you rather make the system feel fairer by smoothing those cliffs, or by lowering top rates and raising more from wealth/investment income instead?
